items.question: About how common is congenital heart disease?
options: About 8 in every 1000 live births
About 8 in every 100 live births
About 8 in every 10 000 live births
About 8 in every 100 000 live births
items.explanation: The guideline gives a prevalence of 8.2 per 1000 live births.

items.question: Overall, what share of cardiac anomalies is identified before birth?
options: Fewer than half
Nearly all
About three quarters
Almost none
items.explanation: Detection varies by region and lesion, but fewer than half of cardiac anomalies are identified before birth.

items.question: A colleague proposes examining the heart in detail only when the pregnancy has a risk factor. What is wrong with this?
options: A high proportion of detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor
Nothing; heart disease is rare without a risk factor
Risk factors cannot be identified before the scan
Detailed examination is only possible in the third trimester
items.explanation: Much of the heart disease that can be detected before birth is in pregnancies with no risk factor and no other anomaly, so every routine scan must be done to standard.

items.question: In a study of missed prenatal diagnoses, what contributed to about half of the misses?
options: Views that did not meet technical criteria
Lesions that developed only after birth
Machines without colour Doppler
Patients who did not attend the scan
items.explanation: Failure to meet technical criteria contributed to about 50% of misses.

items.question: In the same study, a technically adequate view was obtained but the diagnosis was still missed in nearly a third of cases. Why?
options: The abnormal anatomy was not recognised
The lesion was too small to be seen by any examiner
The stored images were lost
The scan was done too late in pregnancy
items.explanation: Failure to recognise abnormal anatomy on an adequate view accounted for 31% of misses. Recognition is a trainable skill.

items.question: Which pair of lesions may show nothing abnormal in the four-chamber plane alone?
options: Transposition of the great arteries and coarctation of the aorta
Atrioventricular septal defect and a single ventricle
A large pericardial effusion and severe cardiomegaly
Dextrocardia and an abnormal cardiac axis
items.explanation: The guideline names transposition and coarctation as lesions that may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone.

items.question: The four-chamber view looks normal. Which view is typically abnormal in tetralogy of Fallot, transposition and common arterial trunk?
options: The three-vessel view
The upper-abdomen view
No axial view; these are found only after birth
The four-chamber view repeated with colour
items.explanation: These lesions can pass the four-chamber view but are typically abnormal in the three-vessel view.

items.question: Which of these is a feature of a screening programme that performs better?
options: A low threshold for referring for fetal echocardiography
Referring only when the diagnosis is certain
Leaving each examiner to choose their own protocol
Limiting the scan to the four-chamber view to save time
items.explanation: Better programmes have feedback-based training, a low referral threshold, standardised protocols and easy access to fetal heart specialists.

items.question: How often is a practice encouraged to review its own detection rates and diagnostic accuracy?
options: Every year
Only after a complaint
Every five years
Once, when the service starts
items.explanation: Annual review of local detection rates and accuracy is encouraged, with further training as needed.

items.question: Which of these factors that affect detection is most directly within the examiner's control?
options: Transducer frequency and examiner skill
Maternal body habitus
Abdominal scars
Amniotic fluid volume
items.explanation: The guideline lists examiner ability and transducer frequency alongside patient factors such as habitus, scars, fluid volume and fetal position.
